title: B2-21 · Recognize the origin of a speaker

blocks.text: B2-21 · Recognize the origin of a speaker
Lesson overview

Now you know the fuṣḥā, the Egyptian, the Levant (passive) and the Moroccan (passive). But the Arab world speaks of many other varieties: the Gulf, Iraq, Sudan, Tunisia, Algeria, Libya and Yemen. You can't learn all of them; But you can learn to recognize them: just a dozen words and some sounds are enough to say, most likely, this speaker comes from the Maghreb or this is an accent of the Gulf. It is a useful skill to understand (know what to expect), to translate (B2-17: The choice of variety is information) and to work with open sources. But it is also a skill to use with caution: an accent indicates a probability, not an identity. In this unit you learn the large dialect areas, a table of traits (G77), a three-step method and the correct way to report a hypothesis on variety. A new character accompanies you: Ġāda, Tunisian journalist. Three weeks, in parallel with MAG-02.

rows: B2 · Module B2.4 Variation and production
B2-17, B2-18; EGY and MAG tracks; B2-09 (modality and certainty)
16–18 hours · three weeks (weeks 236–238), plus the MAG track in separate blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Reference Grammar (G)77), authentic recordings of speakers of different varieties chosen by the tutor (interviews, public videos), sessions with the tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. describe the great dialectal areas of the Arab world;
2. use a table of strokes (sounds, grammar words, verb) to recognize the area of a speaker;
3. to distinguish, at least broadly, the varieties of the Maghreb and those of the Gulf and Iraq;
4. to know what factors make a hypothesis (adaptment, mobility, media, mixed varieties) uncertain;
5. refer a hypothesis on the variety with the correct degree of certainty, in English and Arabic.
Three-week plan.

2. Large areas

rows: What do you know about it?
Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Emirates, Oman; Yemen (variety of its own)

blocks.text: Maghreb Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya; Mauritania (ḥassāniyya) Moroccan passive (track MAG)

A continuum. The areas have no net borders: between two neighbouring cities the differences are small, between Rabat and Baghdad are large. In each country, moreover, there are differences between city and countryside, between speakers of sedentary and Bedouin origins, between generations. The following tables show the most common trends, not rules without exceptions.

How to read the tables. No traits, alone, are certain: but three or four traits that go in the same direction give a solid hypothesis. ṯ and ḏ preserved (as in fuṣḥā) in a dialectal discourse often indicate Iraq, the Gulf or a Bedouin origin; the singular first-person n- indicates the Maghreb; ʿam and šu They point to the Levant.
4. The three-step method

1. Fuṣḥā or dialect? If the speaker uses only fuṣḥā (read or spoken), the origin is mainly felt in pronunciation (ǧ, q, vowels) and in the linking words ( ⁧يعني⁩ , ⁧بس⁩ , ⁧هيك⁩ , ⁧كده⁩ ). The hypothesis remains weak.

3. Sounds and confirmation. Check with two or three pronunciation strokes; search for confirmations in the vocabulary (French loans in the Maghreb, the English in the Gulf) and in the courtesy formulas (ʿaslāma, ahlēn, labas).
5. Pronunciation

Train your ear on minimal differences. The tutor pronounces pairs of words: qāl / ʾāl / gāl; ǧamīl / gamīl / žmīl; ṯalāṯa / talāta / tlāta; kān / čān. For each pair write which variant you have heard and to which area it may belong. Then the tutor reads whole sentences and you indicate only the trait that hit you first. You don't have to imitate: you have to distinguish.

blocks.text: Variety is not identity. The way of speaking says where a person has learned to speak and who he speaks to, not who he is. A hypothesis on variety is formulated in ways (B2-09) and shall be distinguished from the facts.

Notes of use. ⁧شَامِيّ⁩ refers to ⁧بِلَادُ الشَّامِ⁩ , the historic Levant; in the Syrian speech ⁧الشَّام⁩ It's Damascus, too. ⁧بَدَوِيّ⁩ / ⁧حَضَرِيّ⁩ are the terms of Arabic dialectology: the varieties "beduine" often preserve ṯ and ḏ and pronounce q as g; the 'sedentarian's of the big cities simplify them. They have nothing to do with the current way of life of the speaker.
